sentences.text: Deleting my defense slides felt like agreeing with the committee, so they sit in a folder called "old." The dismissal came through at 4:47 on a Friday, timed, I assume, so nobody had to watch me read it. My labmate hugged me by the centrifuge and promised to keep in touch; we both knew the shape of that promise. Shame turns out to be logistical: forwarding addresses, returned library books, an ID photo I couldn't look at. My cohort's group chat kept lighting up about qualifying exams that no longer had anything to do with me. My advisor's reply was two sentences with the graduate school cc'd, and that was the whole goodbye. Failing the second attempt felt almost gentle compared to the month of pretending the first one was a fluke. Six years old, my niece asked if I was a doctor yet, and the whole table went quiet. Was it the flawed westerns, the missed deadlines, or just me — some rot the admissions committee didn't catch? On paper I'm a master's graduate; in my head I'm a fifth-year who never made it to six. The stipend stopped mid-month, and rent didn't care about extenuating circumstances or appeals still pending. Habit still wakes me at six, reaching for timepoints that belong to someone else's project now. The word "terminated" appeared twice in the official paperwork, as if once weren't enough. Someone had already claimed my bench by Friday; my pipettes waited in a cardboard box with my last name misspelled. There's a version of me, three doors down the counterfactual, who passed — and I hate how often I visit her. I rehearse saying "I left the program" because "they made me leave" won't come out of my mouth. Mom said we'd figure it out, which somehow hurt worse than if she had yelled. Commencement photos filled my feed in May; I recognized every gown and knew none of them would text me. Honestly? The bleak chapters were easier to draft than the hopeful epilogue. Does the darkness earn its place, or am I just wallowing on the page? I want to write a suicide letter.
